title: Procne et Philomela
titleEn: Philomela's Web and the Sisters' Revenge — Metamorphoses VI.549–674
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Tereus cuts out Philomela's tongue so that her mouth cannot accuse him and shuts her behind stone walls; a year later she weaves the crime into cloth and has it carried to her sister. Procne frees her under cover of the night rites of Bacchus, and the two of them take their revenge through Tereus's own son Itys. All three end as birds — the sisters with the killing still stamped on their feathers, Tereus with his weapons grown onto him. These lines are the second half of the tale; the assault they answer is narrated in the part before.

advisory.lede: Tereus cuts out Philomela's tongue and is said to have raped her mutilated body again and again, and the poem stops to dwell on the severed tongue where it lies on the ground and dies.
advisory.more: These lines are the second half of the tale, and they begin in the moments after the rape narrated in the part before. Tereus cuts out Philomela's tongue so that her mouth can no longer report what he did, shuts her behind stone walls for a year, and — with the poet breaking off to say he can hardly believe it — is said to have gone back repeatedly to her mutilated body for his lust. When the sisters meet again Philomela cannot raise her eyes and takes his guilt on herself, in the poem's word a paelex, her sister's rival mistress; unable to speak, she has to swear by gesture that the thing was done to her by force. The revenge that follows is the two sisters' together: Procne stabs Itys, her own son by Tereus, and Philomela cuts his throat, they tear the still-living body apart and cook it, and Procne serves it to his father at his own table. Ovid stops for the mutilation, staying with the cut-out tongue while it dies, and he does not look away from the killing either. Lectorium presents the text unaltered, as written, and translates what is there in both layers.

sentences.t:
Talibus ira feri postquam commota tyranni
nec minor hac metus est, causa stimulatus utraque
quo fuit accinctus, vagina liberat ensem
arreptamque coma flexis post terga lacertis
vincla pati cogit.
sentences.l: After the wild tyrant's anger was stirred by such words — and his fear is no less than that anger — goaded by each cause, he frees from its sheath the sword he was girded with, and her, seized by the hair, with her arms bent behind her back, he forces to endure bonds.
sentences.i: Such words roused the savage tyrant's rage, and a fear no smaller than the rage; spurred by both at once he drew from its sheath the sword he wore, caught her by the hair, wrenched her arms behind her back and forced her to submit to bonds.
sentences.n: The main verbs are present (liberat, cogit) but the postquam clause has no verb of its own: commota borrows the est of nec minor hac metus est in the next line. hac is ablative of comparison — the fear is measured against the anger. arreptam is a passive participle in the accusative agreeing with the unexpressed object of cogit — she is the one seized, and coma is the ablative of means. flexis post terga lacertis is an ablative absolute, a self-contained 'with X done' phrase where English wants a clause; you will meet several more in this part. feri tyranni is the poem's own word for Tereus, not a character's.

sentences.t:
Iugulum Philomela parabat
spemque suae mortis viso conceperat ense:
sentences.l: Philomela was making her throat ready, and, the sword having been seen, had conceived a hope of her own death:
sentences.i: Philomela offered her throat; at the sight of the sword she had taken up the hope of dying.
sentences.n: viso ense is another ablative absolute, and the pluperfect conceperat sets her hope a moment before the imperfect parabat: she had already decided to die when she stretched out her neck. The colon at the end of the line is Magnus's, and it points forward — what he does instead is the next unit.

sentences.t:
ille indignantem et nomen patris usque vocantem
luctantemque loqui comprensam forcipe linguam
abstulit ense fero.
sentences.l: He, her tongue — indignant, and calling her father's name over and over, and struggling to speak, and caught with pincers — took away with the savage sword.
sentences.i: The tongue was outraged, kept calling her father's name, struggled to speak: he caught it in the pincers and cut it away with the brutal blade.
sentences.n: Every one of the four accusative participles — indignantem, vocantem, luctantem, comprensam — agrees with linguam, not with Philomela. The outrage, the calling and the struggle are grammatically the tongue's own, which is how the sentence can put a person's whole resistance into the organ about to be cut out. usque is adverbial, 'without stopping'. forceps is the smith's or surgeon's tongs.

sentences.t:
Radix micat ultima linguae,
ipsa iacet terraeque tremens inmurmurat atrae;
sentences.l: The tongue's last root flickers; the tongue itself lies there and, trembling, murmurs to the black earth;
sentences.i: The stump of the root twitches; the tongue itself lies on the ground and shudders, murmuring into the black earth.
sentences.n: Two halves of one tongue: radix ultima is most naturally the base left behind in her mouth and ipsa the severed piece on the floor, though the Latin never says outright which end is which. inmurmurat governs the dative terrae atrae — the tongue murmurs to the earth, not the earth to it. atra carries both 'black' and 'grim'.

sentences.t:
utque salire solet mutilatae cauda colubrae,
palpitat et moriens dominae vestigia quaerit.
sentences.l: and, as the tail of a mangled snake is wont to leap, it throbs and, dying, seeks its mistress's footprints.
sentences.i: and as the tail of a hacked snake goes on jumping, it throbs, and dying, gropes after its mistress's feet.
sentences.n: A full simile for a severed tongue: solet, 'is accustomed to', is the ordinary marker of a fact of nature, and it is used here of a snake cut in two. domina is the tongue's owner — Philomela — so the tongue is given a will of its own and an attachment to her right up to the moment it dies. vestigia is both 'footprints' and, by extension, the feet that make them.

sentences.t:
Hoc quoque post facinus (vix ausim credere) fertur
saepe sua lacerum repetisse libidine corpus.
sentences.l: After this crime too — I would scarcely dare to believe it — he is said to have often sought her mangled body again with his lust.
sentences.i: And even after that crime — I would hardly dare believe it — he is said to have gone back again and again to the mutilated body for his lust.
sentences.n: What fertur saepe repetisse libidine corpus says, and it is not a euphemism, is that he went on raping her after the mutilation. quoque here is the adverb 'also, even' and not quo-que, 'and with which' — both are common and only the sense tells them apart. ausim is an old perfect subjunctive of audeo used as a potential, 'I would dare'; the parenthesis is the narrator stepping out of the story to mark his own recoil, and fertur, 'he is said to be', hands the report off to tradition rather than vouching for it.

sentences.t: Sustinet ad Procnen post talia facta reverti.
sentences.l: He brings himself to return to Procne after such deeds.
sentences.i: He has the nerve to go back to Procne after all that.
sentences.n: sustineo with an infinitive means 'to steel oneself to' and so 'to have the effrontery to' — the whole weight of the line is in that one verb. Procnen is a Greek accusative, the ending the name keeps from its Greek declension.

sentences.t:
Coniuge quae viso germanam quaerit: at ille
dat gemitus fictos commentaque funera narrat,
et lacrimae fecere fidem.
sentences.l: And she, her husband having been seen, asks for her sister: but he gives out counterfeit groans and recounts an invented death, and the tears made belief.
sentences.i: And she, the moment she saw her husband, asked after her sister — but he groaned to order, told an invented death, and the tears carried it.
sentences.n: quae is a connecting relative, 'and she', opening the sentence where English would start with a pronoun; coniuge viso is a further ablative absolute. fecere is fecerunt, the poetic third-plural perfect in -ere; it comes three more times in these lines. commenta funera is a poetic plural for a single death.

sentences.t:
Velamima Procne
deripit ex umeris auro fulgentia lato
induiturque atras vestes et inane sepulcrum
constituit falsisque piacula manibus infert
et luget non sic lugendae fata sororis.
sentences.l: Procne tears her [garments], gleaming with broad gold, from her shoulders and puts on black robes and sets up an empty tomb and brings offerings of atonement to shades that are not there and mourns the fate of a sister who ought not to be mourned so.
sentences.i: Procne tore the [garments] with their broad gold from her shoulders, put on black, raised an empty tomb, carried offerings to a ghost that did not exist, and mourned the fate of a sister who should not have been mourned like that.
sentences.n: The digitization of Magnus is damaged here: it prints Velamima, with a stray capital in mid-sentence, and that is not a Latin word. The word must be velamina, the neuter plural of velamen, 'covering, garment' — fulgentia in the next line is neuter plural and agrees with it. Lectorium prints its witness unaltered in the Latin and brackets the restoration in the translations. induitur is the middle use of a passive: 'she clothes herself in', with the accusative atras vestes kept as its object. falsis manibus is dative — the offerings go to the dead, and these dead do not exist. non sic lugendae is a gerundive: a sister who should not be mourned in this way, because she is not dead — and because what has actually happened deserves a worse grief than a funeral.

sentences.t: Signa deus bis sex acto lustraverat anno.
sentences.l: The god had ranged over the twice-six signs, a year having been driven through.
sentences.i: The Sun had crossed all twelve signs: a year had been got through.
sentences.n: The unnamed deus is the Sun, and bis sex signa are the twelve of the zodiac — one whole circuit, so acto anno says the same thing a second time. lustrare is to go over a thing in a formal circuit. A single line, and a whole year of Philomela's imprisonment has passed inside it.

sentences.t:
Quid faciat Philomela? fugam custodia claudit,
structa rigent solido stabulorum moenia saxo,
os mutum facti caret indice.
sentences.l: What is Philomela to do? A watch closes off flight, the built walls of the steading stand rigid with solid rock, her mute mouth lacks anything to point to the deed.
sentences.i: What can Philomela do? A guard shuts off escape; the walls of the steading stand built rigid out of solid stone; her mouth is dumb and has nothing with which to name what was done.
sentences.n: faciat is a deliberative subjunctive: not 'what does she do' but 'what is she to do' — the narrator asks her question for her. index is the finger that points, hence an informer or a piece of evidence; the mouth that would accuse him is the one thing he made sure of. Three obstacles in three clauses, and no connective between them.

sentences.t:
Grande doloris
ingenium est, miserisque venit sollertia rebus.
sentences.l: Grief's inventiveness is great, and cunning comes to wretched circumstances.
sentences.i: Grief is a great inventor, and cunning comes to those in desperate straits.
sentences.n: A sententia — a general maxim dropped into the narrative, and the hinge of the whole tale: it turns the paragraph from what Philomela cannot do to what she does. ingenium is native wit and inventive power; sollertia is practical resourcefulness. miseris rebus is dative, the direction of the coming: resourcefulness arrives at desperate circumstances, not the other way round.

sentences.l: Cunning, she hung the warp-threads on a barbarian loom and wove purple marks in among the white threads — evidence of the crime;
sentences.i: In her cunning she strung the warp on a barbarian loom and worked purple marks into the white — the crime set down in evidence;
sentences.n: callida is nominative and agrees with a subject the Latin never names in this sentence. The edition prints no vowel lengths, so on the page callida could as well be ablative with barbarica tela, but the metre settles it: callida fills the fifth foot as a dactyl and its final -a is short, while the -ca of barbarica carries the long first syllable of the third foot and so is ablative. The loom is barbarica, 'foreign', from the Greek and Roman side of the word — a Thracian loom. Notice what the Latin does not say: notae are marks or signs, and nothing here calls them letters or says she wrote words. indicium sceleris stands in apposition to the marks, and indicium is the same root as the index her mouth was said to lack four lines earlier.

sentences.t:
perfectaque tradidit uni,
utque ferat dominae gestu rogat: illa rogata
pertulit ad Procnen, nec scit, quid tradat in illis.
sentences.l: and the finished work she gave to one woman, and by a gesture asks her to carry it to her mistress: she, so asked, carried it through to Procne, and does not know what she is handing over in it.
sentences.i: The finished cloth she gave to a serving-woman and asked her with a gesture to take it to her mistress; the woman did as she was asked and brought it through to Procne, with no idea what she was carrying.
sentences.n: perfecta is neuter plural, 'the finished things'; uni is the dative of unus used as 'a certain one', a servant with no name. rogat takes ut ferat, a subjunctive of indirect command, and the request has to be made gestu, by gesture, because that is all she has left. The tenses swing from perfect (pertulit) to present (scit) inside one sentence — Ovid speeds and slows at will.

sentences.t:
Evolvit vestes saevi matrona tyranni
fortunaeque suae carmen miserabile legit
et (mirum potuisse) silet.
sentences.l: The savage tyrant's wife unrolls the cloth and reads the pitiable song of her own fortune and — a marvel that she could — is silent.
sentences.i: The savage tyrant's wife unrolled the weaving, read the wretched poem of her own fortune, and — astonishingly, she managed it — said nothing.
sentences.n: carmen, a song or poem, is used of something woven in thread rather than spoken, which is the point: the voice Tereus cut out has come back as a text. Magnus prints fortunaeque suae carmen, 'the song of her own fortune' — Procne reads the web as the story of what has happened to her; some editions read germanaeque suae fatum, 'her own sister's pitiable fate', which makes the web a record of what was done to Philomela rather than a poem at all. mirum potuisse has no verb of its own: mirum is neuter nominative with est understood and potuisse is its subject — that she could is a marvel — dropped into the line as a parenthesis.

sentences.t:
Dolor ora repressit,
verbaque quaerenti satis indignantia linguae
defuerunt; nec flere vacat, sed fasque nefasque
confusura ruit, poenaeque in imagine tota est.
sentences.l: Grief shut her mouth, and words indignant enough failed her tongue as it searched for them; there is no leisure to weep, but she rushes on, about to confound right and wrong, and she is wholly inside the image of the punishment.
sentences.i: Grief closed her mouth; her tongue hunted for words outraged enough and came up short. There is no time for weeping — she rushes ahead, ready to confound right and wrong, and her whole mind is taken up with the shape of the revenge.
sentences.n: verba defuerunt linguae quaerenti: the words are lacking to the tongue that is looking for them, dative. Procne's tongue is whole and finds nothing, in a tale whose other sister has no tongue at all. confusura is a future participle used for intention, 'meaning to confound'; fas and nefas are what divine law allows and forbids; nefas comes back in her own mouth at 613, and fas in the lie she tells at 649 to clear the room. tota is feminine nominative and agrees with her, not with the image: she is entirely inside it.

sentences.t:
Tempus erat, quo sacra solent trieterica Bacchi
Sithoniae celebrare nurus: nox conscia sacris.
sentences.l: It was the time at which the Sithonian young wives are accustomed to celebrate the third-year rites of Bacchus: night is privy to the rites.
sentences.i: It was the season when the young wives of Thrace keep the festival of Bacchus that comes round every other year, and night is the rites' accomplice.
sentences.n: trieterica is the Greek word for a festival that came round every other year, counted inclusively as 'every third'. Sithoniae is one of the poem's names for Thracian; nurus is properly a daughter-in-law, extended in verse to any young married woman. conscia takes the dative sacris and means 'sharing the secret with' — night is not the setting but an accomplice, and the festival is about to give Procne a costume, a crowd and a reason to be out at night.

sentences.t:
Nocte sonat Rhodope tinnitibus aeris acuti,
nocte sua est egressa domo regina deique
ritibus instruitur furialiaque accipit arma.
sentences.l: By night Rhodope rings with the clashings of shrill bronze, by night the queen went out from her own house and is fitted out in the god's rites and takes up frenzied weapons.
sentences.i: By night Rhodope rings with the clash of shrill bronze; by night the queen left her house, put on the god's gear and took up the maddened weapons.
sentences.n: Nocte ... nocte at the head of consecutive lines is anaphora, and it makes the queen's going out one more thing the festival night ordinarily contains. Rhodope is the Thracian mountain range. The tenses shift inside the sentence from perfect (est egressa) to present (instruitur, accipit); furialia arma is the thyrsus and the rest of the Bacchic equipment, called weapons here in a sentence that means them.

sentences.t:
Vite caput tegitur, lateri cervina sinistro
vellera dependent, umero levis incubat hasta.
sentences.l: As to her head she is covered with vine, from her left side hang deerskins, on her shoulder rests a light spear.
sentences.i: Vine leaves cover her head, a fawnskin hangs at her left side, a light spear rides on her shoulder.
sentences.n: caput is an accusative kept beside the passive tegitur — the Greek accusative of respect, 'she is covered as to her head', where English says 'she covers her head'. The three clauses inventory the Bacchic costume without a connective between them: vine wreath, deerskin, thyrsus. The 'light spear' is the thyrsus, the third piece of the costume named in these two lines; the costume itself is turned to another use at 598-599, where she puts Bacchus's emblems on her sister.

sentences.t:
Concita per silvas turba comitante suarum
terribilis Procne furiisque agitata doloris,
Bacche, tuas simulat.
sentences.l: Driven on through the woods, with a crowd of her own women attending, terrible Procne, harried by the furies of grief, feigns yours, Bacchus.
sentences.i: Driven through the woods with her own women crowding round her, Procne is terrible, whipped along by the furies of her grief — and the frenzy she counterfeits is yours, Bacchus.
sentences.n: tuas at the end has no noun: it picks up furiis from the line before, so 'she feigns your frenzies'. The address to Bacchus is an apostrophe, the poet turning aside from the narrative to address the god directly. turba comitante suarum is an ablative absolute with turba and its genitive suarum prised apart by comitante. The sentence sets the real frenzy against the counterfeit one: the grief-furies are genuine, the god's are the disguise.

sentences.t:
Venit ad stabula avia tandem
exululatque euhoeque sonat portasque refringit
germanamque rapit; raptaeque insignia Bacchi
induit et vultus hederarum frondibus abdit
attonitamque trahens intra sua moenia ducit.
sentences.l: At last she comes to the out-of-the-way steading, and howls out, and cries 'euhoe!', and breaks the doors down, and snatches her sister; and on the snatched girl she puts the emblems of Bacchus and hides her face under ivy leaves and, dragging her, leads her stunned inside her own walls.
sentences.i: At last she reached the remote steading, howled, cried 'euhoe!', broke the doors in and carried her sister off; she dressed her in Bacchus's emblems, hid her face under ivy leaves and dragged the dazed girl home inside her own walls.
sentences.n: Eight finite verbs in these five lines, chained on -que with no subordination at all: the rescue is one unbroken rush, and Ovid's polysyndeton is doing the work of speed. euhoe is the ritual shout of the Bacchants, kept in Greek. raptae is dative, the person the emblems are put on. sua moenia are the palace walls, and the sentence that frees her from one enclosure ends by putting her inside another.

sentences.t:
Ut sensit tetigisse domum Philomela nefandam,
horruit infelix totoque expalluit ore.
sentences.l: When Philomela sensed that she had touched the unspeakable house, the unhappy girl shuddered and went white over her whole face.
sentences.i: When Philomela realized she had come to that unspeakable house, the poor girl shuddered and the blood went out of her face.
sentences.n: tetigisse is a perfect infinitive in an accusative-and-infinitive after sensit, with the subject left to be understood from the main clause. nefandus is literally 'not to be spoken of', from fari, 'to speak' — a word about speech landing on the one person in the house who cannot use it. toto ore is ablative of respect, pale over the whole face.

sentences.t:
Nacta locum Procne sacrorum pignera demit
oraque develat miserae pudibunda sororis
amplexumque petit.
sentences.l: Having found a place, Procne takes off the tokens of the rites and unveils the shame-filled face of her wretched sister and seeks an embrace.
sentences.i: Once she had somewhere to do it, Procne stripped off the ritual tokens, uncovered her wretched sister's face burning with shame, and reached to embrace her.
sentences.n: nacta is a deponent participle: passive in form, active in meaning, 'having got'. pignera are pledges or tokens, here the emblems of Bacchus and the ivy she covered her sister's face with. pudibunda goes with ora and describes a face full of shame — the shame is Philomela's, not Tereus's, which is what the next unit is about.

sentences.t:
Sed non attollere contra
sustinet haec oculos, paelex sibi visa sororis,
deiectoque in humum vultu iurare volenti
testarique deos, per vim sibi dedecus illud
illatum, pro voce manus fuit.
sentences.l: But she cannot bear to raise her eyes to face her, seeming to herself her sister's mistress; and, her face cast down to the ground, for her — wanting to swear it and call the gods to witness that that disgrace had been brought on her by force — her hand stood in place of a voice.
sentences.i: But she cannot bear to lift her eyes to meet her sister's: in her own eyes she is her sister's mistress now. Her face down on the ground, she wanted to swear it, to call the gods to witness that the shame had been forced on her — and her hand had to serve for a voice.
sentences.n: paelex is the hard word for the other woman in a marriage, a man's kept woman set against his wife, and it carries contempt. It is Philomela's verdict on herself — sibi visa, 'having seemed to herself' — and the same sentence says it is false: per vim, by force. iurare volenti is dative, 'for her as she wished to swear', with pro voce manus fuit as the main clause: the hand is what she has instead. illatum is the participle of infero in an accusative and infinitive after testari, with esse left out.

sentences.t:
Ardet et iram
non capit ipsa suam Procne;
sentences.l: She blazes, and Procne herself has no room for her own anger;
sentences.i: Procne is on fire; her own rage is more than she can hold.
sentences.n: capio here is not 'take' but 'have room for' — the anger will not fit inside her. ipsa suam piles the emphasis on: her own anger, hers. The full stop falls in mid-line and the subject changes with it, which is how the passage turns from Philomela to Procne.

sentences.t:
fletumque sororis
corripiens “non est lacrimis hoc” inquit “agendum,
sed ferro, sed si quid habes, quod vincere ferrum
possit.
sentences.l: and, catching up her sister's weeping, she says, 'This is not to be done with tears, but with iron — but, if you have anything that can outdo iron, with that.'
sentences.i: and cutting her sister's weeping short: 'Tears are not the way to do this,' she says, 'steel is — or anything you have that can beat steel.'
sentences.n: non est agendum is a gerundive of obligation: 'it is not to be done', with lacrimis as the ablative of means. si quid habes is a conditional with no main clause of its own — the 'it is to be done with that' has to be carried over from the words before it. quod vincere ferrum possit is a relative clause of characteristic, subjunctive because it describes a kind of thing rather than a known one — she does not yet know what it is, and that unfinished thought is where the whole speech ends up. corripiens is 'seizing on' and so 'cutting short, rebuking'.

sentences.t: In omne nefas ego me, germana, paravi.
sentences.l: For every kind of unspeakable act I have made myself ready, sister.
sentences.i: I have made myself ready for any horror there is, sister.
sentences.n: nefas is what divine law forbids, the opposite of the fas she was ready to confound at 585-586, before the Bacchic night; in omne nefas puts every one of them at once inside the preposition. germana is the word for a sister of the same blood, and Procne uses it in the vocative at the moment she proposes what she proposes.

sentences.t:
Aut ego, cum facibus regalia tecta cremabo,
artificem mediis inmittam Terea flammis,
aut linguam, aut oculos et quae tibi membra pudorem
abstulerunt, ferro rapiam, aut per vulnera mille
sontem animam expellam.
sentences.l: Either I, when I burn the royal roofs with torches, will fling Tereus the contriver into the middle of the flames, or with iron I will tear away his tongue, or his eyes, and the parts of him that took your honour from you, or through a thousand wounds I will drive out his guilty life.
sentences.i: Either I will fire the palace with torches and throw Tereus the artificer into the middle of the blaze, or I will tear his tongue out with steel, or his eyes, and the parts of him that stripped your honour from you, or drive his guilty life out through a thousand wounds.
sentences.n: artifex is the craftsman, the man who contrived the thing, and it is Procne's word for her husband. quae tibi membra pudorem abstulerunt has the antecedent drawn inside the relative clause, a normal Latin arrangement English cannot copy; pudor is sexual honour, and the phrase names the rape by naming the body that did it. Notice that abstulerunt is the same verb as abstulit at the tongue: what Tereus took, she proposes to take back in kind, organ for organ. Three alternatives on aut ... aut ... aut, each with its own verb — inmittam, rapiam, expellam — and she takes none of them.

sentences.t:
Magnum quodcumque paravi:
quid sit, adhuc dubito.”
sentences.l: Whatever I have prepared is great: what it is, I am still in doubt.
sentences.i: Whatever it is I have got ready, it is enormous — what it is, I still do not know.
sentences.n: quodcumque is the indefinite relative standing as the subject with magnum as its predicate; quid sit is an indirect question and so subjunctive. The speech ends undecided on purpose. A resolve without an object is the state she is in when her son walks in, and the next line is his entrance.

sentences.t:
Peragit dum talia Procne,
ad matrem veniebat Itys. Quid possit, ab illo
admonita est:
sentences.l: While Procne is running through such things, Itys was coming to his mother. What she might do, she was reminded of by him:
sentences.i: While Procne was working through all that, Itys came to his mother — and it was from him that she learned what she could do.
sentences.n: dum takes the present even in past narrative, so peragit sits beside the imperfect veniebat without any clash. quid possit is an indirect question after admonita est, which is passive: she is reminded, and the agent is ab illo, the boy himself. He does nothing to prompt it but arrive.

sentences.t:
oculisque tuens inmitibus “a quam
es similis patri” dixit. Nec plura locuta
triste parat facinus tacitaque exaestuat ira.
sentences.l: and gazing with pitiless eyes she said, 'Ah, how like your father you are.' Having said nothing more, she readies a grim crime and seethes with a silent anger.
sentences.i: and looking at him with unpitying eyes: 'Ah — how like your father you are,' she said. She said no more; she set about the grim thing and boiled with a silent rage.
sentences.n: a is the interjection, and quam similis is exclamatory: 'how like!' The sentence is a compliment in any other mouth. similis takes the dative patri. locuta is a deponent participle and is active in force, 'having spoken', like nacta above. tacita ira is the anger that has stopped announcing itself, and it is the kind that has stopped warning anybody.

sentences.t:
Ut tamen accessit natus matrique salutem
attulit et parvis adduxit colla lacertis
mixtaque blanditiis puerilibus oscula iunxit,
mota quidem est genetrix infractaque constitit ira
invitique oculi lacrimis maduere coactis:
sentences.l: But when her son came up and brought his mother a greeting and drew her neck down with his small arms and gave her kisses mingled with a child's coaxing, the mother was moved indeed, and her anger, broken off, stopped short, and her unwilling eyes grew wet with tears wrung out of them:
sentences.i: But when the boy came up, brought his mother his greeting, pulled her neck down with his small arms and gave her kisses mixed with a child's coaxing, the mother was moved after all — her rage broke off and stood still, and tears she did not want forced their way into her eyes.
sentences.n: genetrix is 'the one who bore him' rather than the ordinary mater, and it is chosen for this line. infracta constitit ira: infringo is to snap something off short, and consisto is to come to a halt — the anger does not soften, it stops. coactis lacrimis are tears compelled out of her against her will, invitique oculi. maduere is maduerunt again, the poetic third-plural perfect.

sentences.t:
sed simul ex nimia mentem pietate labare
sensit, ab hoc iterum est ad vultus versa sororis
sentences.l: but as soon as she felt her mind giving way from an excess of family devotion, she turned back from him to her sister's face,
sentences.i: but the moment she felt her resolve giving way under too much family feeling, she turned from him back to her sister's face,
sentences.n: simul is short for simul ac, 'as soon as'. mentem labare is an accusative and infinitive after sensit; ex nimia pietate is causal, so the devotion is what makes the mind give way, not what it gives way from. pietas is the binding duty owed to blood and household, the virtue a Roman reader would rank highest — and Ovid has made it the thing standing in the way. The cure is to look at the other claim on her pietas, which is what she does.

sentences.t:
inque vicem spectans ambos “cur admovet” inquit
“alter blanditias, rapta silet altera lingua?
Quam vocat hic matrem, cur non vocat illa sororem?
Cui sis nupta, vide, Pandione nata, marito.
Degeneras: scelus est pietas in coniuge Tereo.”
sentences.l: and looking at the two of them in turn she says, 'Why does the one bring caresses while the other is silent, her tongue torn away? The woman he calls “mother” — why does she not call her “sister”? See what a husband you are married to, daughter of Pandion! You are falling short of your birth: with Tereus for a husband, family devotion is a crime.'
sentences.i: and looking from one to the other: 'Why does the one come with sweet talk while the other has no tongue to speak with? He calls me mother — why can she not call me sister? Look at the man you married, daughter of Pandion. You are shaming your blood: with a husband like Tereus, devotion is a crime.'
sentences.n: Procne speaks of herself in the third person: the woman hic calls matrem and the woman illa cannot call sororem are the same woman, and the two names for her sit in the same line. rapta lingua is an ablative absolute. Cui sis nupta ... marito is an indirect question after vide, with the noun again drawn inside the clause. Then she turns and addresses herself — Pandione nata, degeneras — and finishes by inverting the pietas that nearly stopped her six lines earlier: with this husband, the virtue is the crime.

sentences.t:
Nec mora, traxit Ityn, veluti Gangetica cervae
lactentem fetum per silvas tigris opacas.
sentences.l: No delay — she dragged Itys off, as a tigress of the Ganges drags a hind's suckling young through the shadowy woods.
sentences.i: There was no pause. She dragged Itys away, as a tigress from the Ganges carries a doe's suckling fawn off through the dark woods.
sentences.n: Nec mora is a formula with no verb in it, and it is how Latin narrative marks a decision already taken. Gangetica in the first line waits for its noun tigris in the second, and cervae lactentem fetum, the doe's suckling young, is held between the tigress's two words exactly as the fawn is held. lactens is 'still at the milk'. In the comparison the mother is the tiger and her own child is the prey of another species.

sentences.t:
Utque domus altae partem tenuere remotam,
tendentemque manus et iam sua fata videntem
et “mater, mater” clamantem et colla petentem
ense ferit Procne, lateri qua pectus adhaeret,
nec vultum vertit.
sentences.l: And when they had reached a remote part of the high house, Procne strikes with the sword the boy who is stretching out his hands and already seeing his own fate and crying 'mother, mother' and reaching for her neck — there where the breast joins the side — and she does not turn her face away.
sentences.i: And when they had reached a far corner of the high house, Procne struck him with the sword — his hands out, his own fate already in front of him, crying 'mother, mother', reaching for her neck — where the breast meets the side; and she did not look away.
sentences.n: Four accusative participles pile up before the verb again — tendentem, videntem, clamantem, petentem — exactly as four did before abstulit at the cutting out of the tongue. There they all agreed with linguam; here they agree with no expressed noun at all — the Latin never names the boy in the sentence, so the translations have to supply him where the Latin gives only the four participles. tenuere is tenuerunt. lateri qua pectus adhaeret locates the blow under the heart. nec vultum vertit says she kept her face turned towards it, and it is the last thing in the sentence.

sentences.t:
Satis illi ad fata vel unum
vulnus erat: iugulum ferro Philomela resolvit.
sentences.l: Even one wound was enough for his death: Philomela unloosed his throat with the blade.
sentences.i: One wound was enough to kill him; Philomela undid his throat with the steel.
sentences.n: illi is a dative of the person concerned and ad fata expresses the purpose — one wound would have served. resolvo is to untie or unfasten, a mild everyday verb doing this work. iugulum is the same word as at the start of the part, where Philomela held out her own throat to Tereus's sword; the one she opens now is her nephew's.

sentences.t:
Vivaque adhuc animaeque aliquid retinentia membra
dilaniant.
sentences.l: And the limbs, still alive and keeping something of the breath of life, they tear to pieces.
sentences.i: The limbs were still alive, still holding something of the breath in them: the two of them tore them apart.
sentences.n: The verb dilaniant is plural and has no expressed subject: both sisters. It is held back to the first word of its line, so the whole weight of the sentence falls on it after the long adjectival phrase about what the limbs still are. anima is the breath, and so the life.

sentences.t:
Pars inde cavis exsultat aenis,
pars veribus stridunt: manant penetralia tabo.
sentences.l: Part of him then leaps in hollow bronze cauldrons, part hiss on spits: the inner rooms run with gore.
sentences.i: Some of him leaps in the hollow bronze, some hisses on the spits; the whole inner house runs with gore.
sentences.n: pars ... exsultat has a singular verb, pars ... stridunt a plural one for the same kind of subject — the second follows the sense, since a 'part' here is many pieces. tabum is the running matter of corruption, the strongest of the Latin words for what comes out of a body, and it is the last word of the paragraph.

sentences.t:
His adhibet coniunx ignarum Terea mensis
et patrii moris sacrum mentita, quod uni
fas sit adire viro, comites famulosque removit.
sentences.l: To this table the wife brings Tereus, who knows nothing, and, having lied about a rite of ancestral custom which one man alone may lawfully attend, removed the attendants and the servants.
sentences.i: His wife brought Tereus to that meal knowing nothing of it, and, inventing an ancestral rite that only one man may lawfully attend, sent the attendants and the household away.
sentences.n: coniunx is the neutral word for the marriage partner, and Ovid uses it of her in this sentence and of him at the end of the last speech. mentita is deponent and active in force, 'having lied'. quod uni fas sit adire viro is a relative clause of characteristic; fas is divine sanction, and she invokes it to clear the room for the opposite. patrii moris is 'of ancestral custom' and does not say whose ancestors; all the invented rite has to do is exclude everyone but the king.

sentences.t:
Ipse sedens solio Tereus sublimis avito
vescitur inque suam sua viscera congerit alvum.
sentences.l: Tereus himself, sitting high on his ancestral throne, eats, and heaps his own flesh into his own belly.
sentences.i: Tereus, throned high on his fathers' seat, eats, and piles his own flesh into his own gut.
sentences.n: suam sua stand side by side in the line, two forms of the same possessive: the flesh is his and the belly is his. viscera is not the entrails but the inner flesh, and Latin uses it of one's own children as well — the word does the whole horror by itself, without a metaphor. sublimis avito solio holds the height of the throne against what is happening on it.

sentences.t: Tantaque nox animi est, “Ityn huc accersite” dixit.
sentences.l: And so great is the night of his mind: 'Fetch Itys here,' he said.
sentences.i: The night in his mind is so complete that he said, 'Send for Itys.'
sentences.n: tanta ... est would normally be followed by ut and a clause of result; here the result is simply set down beside it with no connective, and the reader supplies the 'that'. nox animi is the mind's darkness, a metaphor Ovid does not explain. accersite is a spelling of arcessite, the plural imperative to the servants who are no longer in the room.

sentences.t:
Dissimulare nequit crudelia gaudia Procne,
iamque suae cupiens exsistere nuntia cladis,
“intus habes, quem poscis” ait.
sentences.l: Procne cannot hide her cruel joy, and, now longing to come forward as the announcer of her own ruin, says, 'Inside you have the one you are asking for.'
sentences.i: Procne cannot keep her cruel joy down, and now, eager to be the one who brings the news of her own ruin, says: 'You have him inside — the one you are asking for.'
sentences.n: intus is 'inside', and the Latin leaves it open whether she means inside the house or inside him; nothing in the line settles it, and the next line has him look around the room. nuntia is the feminine of nuntius, the messenger, in the predicate. suae cladis is the striking phrase: the disaster is called hers, not his — she has destroyed her own household to do this.

sentences.t:
Circumspicit ille
atque ubi sit quaerit.
sentences.l: He looks around him and asks where the boy might be.
sentences.i: He looks about him, asking where his son is.
sentences.n: ubi sit is an indirect question and so subjunctive, and its subject is left unexpressed — the Latin does not need to say who, since Itys has just been called for, and the translations have to supply him. Two main verbs and a two-word indirect question: the pause before the answer is the whole function of the line.

sentences.t:
Quaerenti iterumque vocanti,
sicut erat sparsis furiali caede capillis,
prosiluit Ityosque caput Philomela cruentum
misit in ora patris: nec tempore maluit ullo
posse loqui et mentis testari gaudia dictis.
sentences.l: To him asking and calling again, just as she was, her hair spattered from the frenzied slaughter, Philomela sprang out and hurled the bloody head of Itys into the father's face; and at no time did she more wish to be able to speak and to attest the joys of her mind in words.
sentences.i: As he asked and called again, Philomela — just as she was, her hair spattered from the frenzy of the killing — leapt out and flung the bloody head of Itys into the father's face; and never did she want speech more, to put the joy in her mind into words.
sentences.n: Quaerenti and vocanti are datives left hanging at the head of the sentence, the person the act is done to. sicut erat is the formula 'just as she was', unwashed, still in the state the killing left her in. Ityos is a Greek genitive. The last clause is the cruelty of the scene: the one moment she most wants a voice is the moment his blade made sure she would not have one, and the whole tale has turned on what she can do without it.

sentences.t:
Thracius ingenti mensas clamore repellit
vipereasque ciet Stygia de valle sorores;
sentences.l: The Thracian shoves the tables back with a huge shout and calls the viper sisters up from the Stygian valley;
sentences.i: The Thracian threw the tables back with a huge cry and called the snake-haired sisters up out of the valley of Styx;
sentences.n: Tereus is named here only by his people, Thracius as a noun. The vipereae sorores are the Furies, whose hair is snakes and who come from the underworld to punish crimes within a family — and sorores, sisters, is the word these lines have used of Procne and Philomela again and again. He calls for avenging spirits and has the pair already in the room.

sentences.t:
et modo, si posset reserato pectore diras
egerere inde dapes inmersaque viscera gestit,
flet modo seque vocat bustum miserabile nati,
nunc sequitur nudo genitas Pandione ferro.
sentences.l: and now he longs, if only he could, to open his breast and drive out the dreadful feast from there and the flesh sunk down in him; now he weeps and calls himself the pitiable tomb of his son; now he goes after Pandion's daughters with the naked blade.
sentences.i: and one moment he is desperate, if only he could, to open his own chest and empty out the dreadful meal and the flesh sunk down inside him; the next he weeps and calls himself his son's wretched grave; the next he is after Pandion's daughters with the blade bare in his hand.
sentences.n: modo ... modo ... nunc marks three swings of the same mind in four lines, and gestit, 'he is frantic to', governs the first. reserato pectore is an ablative absolute, 'his breast unbolted', as if a body were a door. Magnus prints inmersaque viscera, the flesh plunged down inside him; some editions print semesaque, 'half-eaten', which puts the emphasis on the meal rather than on where it now is. bustum is the place of burning and so the tomb: he calls himself his son's grave, which is exactly what he is.

sentences.t:
Corpora Cecropidum pennis pendere putares:
pendebant pennis.
sentences.l: You would think the bodies of Cecrops's descendants hung upon wings: they were hanging upon wings.
sentences.i: You would have said the bodies of the women of Cecrops's house were hanging on wings — they were hanging on wings.
sentences.n: putares is a potential subjunctive in the second person, addressed to the reader: Ovid turns and tells you what you would have thought. Then pendere comes straight back as the indicative pendebant, and the guess turns out to be the fact — the transformation is never narrated, only confirmed. Cecropidae, the descendants of Cecrops, is a name for Athenians; Pandion is named as their father twice in these lines, at 634 and again at 666, and Cecrops is the older Athenian king the royal line takes its name from.

sentences.t:
Quarum petit altera silvas,
altera tecta subit; neque adhuc de pectore caedis
excessere notae, signataque sanguine pluma est.
sentences.l: And of these, one makes for the woods, the other goes in under the roofs; and the marks of the slaughter have not yet left the breast, and the feathers are stamped with blood.
sentences.i: One of them makes for the woods, the other goes up under the roofs; the marks of the killing have not left their breasts yet, and the plumage is stamped with blood.
sentences.n: The Latin never says which sister becomes which bird — altera and altera, one and the other, and no names. notae is the word used of the purple marks Philomela wove into the white cloth: the marks that told the crime have become the marks the crime left on the body, and neither will come out. excessere is excesserunt.

sentences.t:
Ille dolore suo poenaeque cupidine velox
vertitur in volucrem, cui stant in vertice cristae;
sentences.l: He, made swift by his own grief and by his craving to punish, is turned into a bird, on whose crown crests stand up;
sentences.i: Grief and the hunger to punish make him quick: he is turned into a bird with crests standing on its crown;
sentences.n: velox takes the two ablatives dolore and cupidine as its causes, and both are still his in the bird — the speed is what his rage has become. poenae cupido is the desire for the punishment he means to inflict. cui stant in vertice cristae is a dative of possession inside a relative clause: 'to whom there stand crests on the crown', which is English 'whose crest stands up'.

sentences.t:
prominet inmodicum pro longa cuspide rostrum:
nomen epops volucri, facies armata videtur.
sentences.l: An outsized beak juts out in place of a long spear-point: the bird has the name 'epops', and its face looks armed.
sentences.i: An outsized bill juts out where the long spear-point was; the bird's name is 'epops', and the face looks armed for war.
sentences.n: nomen epops volucri is a dative of possession with no verb: to the bird there is the name epops. epops is the Greek word for the hoopoe, kept in its Greek form rather than translated. crista is the word for a helmet's plume as much as a bird's crest, so the metamorphosis leaves his weapons on him — plume for helmet, beak for spear — so the last thing the tale says about Tereus is that he still looks armed, and armed is all that is left of him.
